title: Distributed Tracing
description: Understand trace context propagation, span trees, tools like Jaeger and Zipkin, and strategies for sampling in high-throughput systems.

segments.text: In a monolith, a stack trace shows you the full request path. In microservices, a single user request might touch ten services. When something is slow, which service is the bottleneck? Distributed tracing gives you the answer.

A trace represents the entire journey of a request through your system. It starts when the request enters your API gateway and ends when the response leaves. Every service call, database query, and cache lookup along the way is captured as a span within that trace.

A span represents a single operation: a service call, a database query, a cache lookup. Each span has a start time, duration, status, and metadata. Spans form a tree — the root span is the initial request, child spans are the downstream calls it makes.

The magic is context propagation. When service A calls service B, it passes a trace ID and span ID in HTTP headers. Service B creates a child span linked to A's span. This threading of context through every call is what stitches the whole trace together.
segments.thought_prompt: What happens if one service doesn't propagate the trace context? What breaks?

segments.text: The trace viewer shows spans as a waterfall diagram. Each span is a horizontal bar. Its position shows when it started, its width shows how long it took. You can instantly see which span is the bottleneck — it's the widest bar in the waterfall.

Jaeger, created by Uber, and Zipkin, created by Twitter, are the two most popular tracing systems. Both collect spans from your services, store them, and provide UIs to search and visualize traces. They follow the OpenTelemetry standard for interoperability.

Instrumentation is how you add tracing to your code. With OpenTelemetry SDKs, most frameworks auto-instrument HTTP calls, database queries, and gRPC calls. You get tracing almost for free — just add the SDK and configure an exporter.

At high throughput, tracing every request generates enormous data volumes. A service handling 100,000 requests per second producing traces for each one would overwhelm your storage. This is where sampling comes in — you trace a representative subset.
segments.thought_prompt: If you only trace 1% of requests, how do you make sure you capture the interesting failures?

segments.text: Head-based sampling decides at the start whether to trace the request — simple but you might miss errors. Tail-based sampling decides after the request completes, keeping only interesting traces like errors or slow requests. Tail-based is smarter but requires buffering all spans temporarily.

In practice, add custom span tags for business context: user ID, order ID, feature flag. These make traces searchable and meaningful. Without business context, you're looking at anonymous service calls with no way to connect them to user-reported issues.

Distributed tracing completes the observability picture. Logs tell you what happened, metrics tell you the aggregates, and traces tell you the exact path a request took and where it slowed down. Together, they give you full visibility into your distributed system.
